front.title: Hop Limit for Requests Forwarded Between Media over QUIC Relays

abstract.t: A Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT) relay that cannot serve a request locally can forward it to an upstream relay. MOQT defines no bound on how many times a request may be forwarded, so a misconfigured set of relays can forward one request around a cycle until a timeout or resource limit ends it. This document defines a HOP_LIMIT Message Parameter, negotiated with a Setup Option, that each relay decrements when it forwards a request, and a HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error that a relay returns when the limit is exhausted. It complements extensions that prevent loops in namespace advertisement by covering requests that relays forward without an advertisement.

note.title: Note to Readers
note.t: Discussion of this document takes place on the Media Over QUIC Working Group mailing list (moq@ietf.org).
This document targets draft-ietf-moq-transport-22. Section references to are to that version.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: MOQT relays form distribution trees: a relay that has no local publisher or cached copy for a requested track forwards the request toward one (). Many deployments choose where to forward by configuration rather than by advertisement, as content delivery networks pull from an origin. An edge relay names a parent for a set of namespaces, the parent names its own, and so on.

Configuration produces cycles. If relay A is configured to forward a namespace to relay B, and B to A, a SUBSCRIBE for a track that neither holds is forwarded from A to B to A indefinitely. Each forward consumes a request stream, Request ID credit, and state on both relays. Neither relay can detect the cycle locally: a request that arrives from a peer relay is the same message, on the same kind of session, as one from an end subscriber.

notes that PUBLISH_NAMESPACE "does not protect against loops" () and places relay-to-relay interconnection out of scope (). This document does not define relay interconnection or routing. It adds one loop-safety property to any interconnection that forwards MOQT requests between relays: a request can be forwarded through at most a bounded number of relays, after which it fails with a specific error. The technique is the Time to Live of , the Hop Limit of , and the Max-Forwards header of , applied to MOQT requests.

section.name: Relationship to the Cluster Extension
section.t: prevents loops in namespace advertisements by carrying the path an advertisement has traversed, and it selects the upstream for a request from those advertisements. That covers meshes in which relays learn routes from PUBLISH_NAMESPACE and NAMESPACE.

This document covers requests that a relay forwards without an advertisement to follow: to a configured parent, to an origin chosen by policy, or after following a REDIRECT. The two mechanisms are independent and can be negotiated together. A relay that negotiates both applies the path rules of when it selects an upstream, and the hop limit of this document when it forwards the request.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the terms defined in . In addition:

dd.t: A request that a relay sends to an upstream peer because it received a request from a downstream peer that it could not satisfy from local state. This includes upstream FETCHes that a relay issues to fill gaps in a downstream FETCH ().
A SUBSCRIBE (), FETCH (), TRACK_STATUS (), SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE () or SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS () message. These are the requests a relay forwards upstream on behalf of a downstream peer.
The number of further relays to which a request may be forwarded, computed by a relay as described in .
A relay's configured maximum for the remaining hop limit ().

section.name: Negotiation
section.t: requires an endpoint to close the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION when it receives a Message Parameter that was not defined in the negotiated version or negotiated through Setup Options (). The HOP_LIMIT parameter is therefore sent only on sessions where this extension is negotiated.
An endpoint declares support by including the HOP_LIMIT_SUPPORTED Setup Option in its SETUP message ():

figure.title: HOP_LIMIT_SUPPORTED Setup Option

section.t: The Option Type is odd, so the option is length-prefixed, and its value is empty: presence alone declares support, as described in . An endpoint that receives HOP_LIMIT_SUPPORTED with a non-empty value MUST close the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION. An endpoint MUST NOT include the option more than once.

The extension is negotiated on a session when both endpoints included HOP_LIMIT_SUPPORTED in SETUP. Negotiation is per session: a relay MUST NOT infer that a peer supports the extension on one session because it did on another.

Relays that forward covered requests SHOULD declare support. Endpoints that never forward requests, such as end subscribers and original publishers, MAY declare support; doing so lets them receive HOP_LIMIT without a session error ().
This extension can be used with draft-ietf-moq-transport-22 and later versions that keep the extension negotiation of .

section.name: The HOP_LIMIT Parameter
section.t: HOP_LIMIT (Parameter Type TBD2) is a Message Parameter whose value is a varint (): the number of further relays to which the request carrying it may be forwarded.

HOP_LIMIT MAY appear in any covered request. It MUST NOT appear in any other message, including REQUEST_UPDATE and the FILL_PARAMETERS parameter (). A relay's budget for a request is fixed when the request is made; an update cannot extend it. An endpoint that receives HOP_LIMIT in any other message MUST close the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION, as requires.
A covered request MUST NOT contain more than one HOP_LIMIT parameter.
An endpoint MUST NOT send HOP_LIMIT on a session where the extension was not negotiated, and a receiver of HOP_LIMIT on such a session closes the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION as requires.
Like every Message Parameter, HOP_LIMIT applies to one hop and is not copied to the forwarded request (). A relay computes the value it sends from the value it received.

section.name: Computing the Remaining Hop Limit
section.t: When a relay receives a covered request, it computes the remaining hop limit:

list.t: If the request carries no HOP_LIMIT, the remaining hop limit is MAX_HOP_LIMIT. This is the case for a request from an end subscriber, or from a peer that did not negotiate the extension.
If the request carries HOP_LIMIT, the remaining hop limit is the smaller of its value and MAX_HOP_LIMIT.

section.t: A relay MUST NOT compute a remaining hop limit greater than MAX_HOP_LIMIT. Clamping on receipt means a peer cannot raise another relay's bound, and a cycle through relays with different maximums is bounded by the smallest.

section.name: Serving a Request Without Forwarding
section.t: A relay that can satisfy a covered request without forwarding it, from a local publisher, its cache, or an Established upstream subscription, does so as specifies. The remaining hop limit is not consumed and has no effect on the response.

section.name: Forwarding a Request
section.t: A relay that would forward a covered request upstream first checks the remaining hop limit:

list.t: If the remaining hop limit is zero, the relay MUST NOT forward the request. It MUST respond to the downstream request with REQUEST_ERROR and error code HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED ().
Otherwise, the relay MAY forward the request. If the upstream session negotiated the extension, the forwarded request MUST carry HOP_LIMIT with a value one less than the remaining hop limit.

section.t: Every upstream request that a relay issues to satisfy one downstream request carries the same value. This includes the several upstream FETCHes that one downstream FETCH can generate (), and requests retried to a different upstream after a failure.

A relay MUST NOT send a HOP_LIMIT value greater than or equal to the remaining hop limit of the downstream request that caused it. The value strictly decreases with each forward, so a request cannot be forwarded more than MAX_HOP_LIMIT times through relays that implement this extension, however they are connected.

section.name: Aggregated Requests
section.t: A relay MAY satisfy a new downstream request by attaching it to an upstream request it already sent for the same track or namespace prefix (). Attaching consumes no hop limit, but it can create a cycle that the hop limit alone does not end. Suppose relay A forwards a SUBSCRIBE to B and is waiting for the reply. B forwards it back to A, and A attaches it to its own pending upstream request. A now waits for B and B waits for A. A relay sends SUBSCRIBE_OK only once its upstream subscription is Established (), so both wait until a timeout ends the request.

To prevent this, a relay MUST NOT attach a downstream covered request to a pending upstream request if the downstream request's remaining hop limit is smaller than the remaining hop limit of the downstream request that caused the pending one. A request that has gone around a cycle always returns with a smaller remaining hop limit than it left with, so it is forwarded again rather than attached, and it fails with HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED after a bounded number of forwards. That error then completes the pending requests in the cycle, as describes.

A pending upstream request is one that has been sent and has not received SUBSCRIBE_OK, FETCH_OK, REQUEST_OK, TRACK_STATUS_OK, or REQUEST_ERROR. A relay MAY attach any downstream request to an Established upstream subscription. An Established subscription means a publisher was found, so there is no cycle to break.

When relays at different depths request the same track at the same time, this rule can make a relay send two upstream requests where it would have sent one. The duplicate lasts only while the first request is pending.

section.name: Following Redirects
section.t: A relay that follows a REDIRECT () from upstream is still forwarding the original downstream request. The new request MUST carry the same HOP_LIMIT value as the request that was redirected, and the relay MUST NOT reset the remaining hop limit to MAX_HOP_LIMIT. A relay SHOULD bound the number of redirects it follows for one downstream request, because a redirect does not consume hop limit at the relay that follows it.

section.name: Upstream Peers Without the Extension
section.t: A relay MAY forward a covered request to an upstream peer that did not negotiate the extension. It sends the request without HOP_LIMIT, and that peer computes MAX_HOP_LIMIT for the request. The bound therefore holds across each run of consecutive relays that implement this extension, and a cycle passes through a relay that does not implement it starts over at that relay's MAX_HOP_LIMIT.
A cycle made only of relays that implement this extension is always bounded. Operators that need the bound across their whole topology deploy the extension on every relay that can forward requests.

section.name: Endpoints That Are Not Relays
section.t: An end subscriber SHOULD NOT send HOP_LIMIT. It has forwarded nothing, and a relay treats an absent HOP_LIMIT as MAX_HOP_LIMIT.
An original publisher, or any endpoint that serves a covered request without forwarding it, ignores a received HOP_LIMIT, provided the extension was negotiated on that session.

section.name: Choosing MAX_HOP_LIMIT
section.t: MAX_HOP_LIMIT SHOULD be configurable. It should be at least the number of upstream relays on the longest legitimate path from an edge relay to an original publisher. For example, a topology with an edge tier, one interior tier and an origin forwards a request at most twice, from the edge to the interior relay and from the interior relay to the origin. It needs a MAX_HOP_LIMIT of 2.

Fan-out grows multiplicatively with each tier while latency grows additively, so deep relay trees are uncommon. Implementations SHOULD use a small default; this document RECOMMENDS a default of 3. A larger value lengthens the work a cycle does before it fails, and does nothing for topologies without cycles.
All relays in a deployment SHOULD use the same MAX_HOP_LIMIT. Because each relay clamps on receipt, a relay with a smaller value shortens the paths that pass through it.

section.name: Error Handling
section.t: A relay that refuses to forward a request because its remaining hop limit is zero responds with REQUEST_ERROR () and the error code HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (TBD3). The relay SHOULD set Retry Interval to 0. Retrying the same request through the same topology fails the same way.
HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED indicates a configuration problem, not a protocol violation, and MUST NOT cause either endpoint to close the session.

A relay that receives HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED for an upstream request SHOULD respond with HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED to every downstream request that is waiting for it, including requests attached under . New error codes can be used without negotiation, and a receiver that does not recognize the code treats it as INTERNAL_ERROR (). A relay can therefore send HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED to a downstream peer whether or not that peer negotiated this extension.

A relay MAY cache a HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED response and use it for matching requests that arrive with the same or a smaller remaining hop limit. It SHOULD NOT keep the cached response longer than a short, configured interval, because the misconfiguration that caused it may be corrected at any time.
A HOP_LIMIT value that is not a valid varint is a malformed control message, which treats as a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

section.name: Operational Considerations
section.t: A HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED response is the first sign of a cycle or of a path deeper than MAX_HOP_LIMIT. Relays SHOULD log it with the track or namespace and the upstream peer, and SHOULD count it in their metrics, so that operators can find the misconfiguration.
The extension bounds the work a cycle causes but does not repair the cycle. Subscribers to an affected namespace receive an error until the configuration is corrected.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Without a hop limit, one downstream request into a cycle of relays causes an unbounded number of forwarded requests, each holding a request stream and state on two relays. With this extension, one downstream request causes at most MAX_HOP_LIMIT forwards through relays that implement it, multiplied by any retries and redirects each relay follows (, ). Implementations SHOULD bound retries and redirects for this reason.

A peer can send a smaller HOP_LIMIT than it received, which only makes its own requests fail sooner. It cannot raise another relay's bound, because each relay clamps the value on receipt (). A malicious relay can always issue new requests of its own, so this extension protects against misconfiguration and limits amplification through honest relays. It does not protect against a hostile relay.

The HOP_LIMIT value tells the upstream peer how many more forwards a request may take, which hints at the downstream peer's position in a topology. A relay that considers this sensitive can send the same value on every request it forwards across a trust boundary, at the cost of a weaker bound for cycles that cross the boundary.
The considerations of for relays also apply.

dd.t: Implements this document for SUBSCRIBE on draft-ietf-moq-transport-22 sessions, using the provisional values 0x40C51, 0x40C52 and 0x37. It sends HOP_LIMIT_SUPPORTED in its own SETUP and uses HOP_LIMIT only on a session where the peer sent it too. It closes the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION if HOP_LIMIT_SUPPORTED carries a value, or if HOP_LIMIT appears on a session that did not negotiate it. MAX_HOP_LIMIT is configurable and defaults to 3. An absent HOP_LIMIT means MAX_HOP_LIMIT, and a larger value is clamped to it. The relay refuses to forward at zero with HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED and a Retry Interval of 0, and it logs and counts the refusal. Each forward carries one less than the remaining hop limit. A HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED from upstream is passed to every downstream subscriber waiting on that request. The relay applies the aggregation rule of to pending upstream subscriptions. It also carries the remaining hop limit in a vendor parameter, 0x4D50, which it uses on draft-ietf-moq-transport-19 sessions and towards peers that did not negotiate this extension but did enable MOQOM's vendor parameters. When a request carries both parameters, the smaller value is used. On draft-ietf-moq-transport-19 sessions an exhausted limit is answered with DOES_NOT_EXIST, because that version has no HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED code. The relay forwards only SUBSCRIBE between relays: it serves FETCH from its own cache and does not forward TRACK_STATUS, SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE or SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS. It does not follow REDIRECT; it passes the response to the downstream subscriber. It caches no HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED response. Integration tests run chains of three relays and a cycle of two. They show that a request is served with enough hop limit remaining, and that HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED is returned at the relay where the limit reaches zero and propagated to the subscriber. They also show that the session stays open after the error, and that a cycle ends in HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED.
Does not offer HOP_LIMIT_SUPPORTED, so relays never send it HOP_LIMIT. It accepts the vendor parameter 0x4D50 as an original publisher and never sends it.

abstract.t: This document defines Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT), a publish/ subscribe protocol that runs over QUIC and WebTransport. MOQT leverages the features of these transports, such as streams, datagrams, priorities, and partial reliability. MOQT operates both point-to-point and through intermediate relays, enabling scalable low-latency delivery. Despite its name, MOQT is media agnostic and can be used for a wide range of use cases.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

This document defines a clustering extension for MoQ Transport [moqt], used to build a mesh of relays. Each namespace advertisement carries the list of Hop IDs it has passed through, starting with the original publisher, and the accumulated cost of that path. A receiver uses the list to detect loops and to tell which advertisements come from the same publisher, and the cost to choose between paths. Each endpoint declares its own Hop ID at setup, so a peer never advertises or serves it a path that already passed through it.
This document specifies version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6). It obsoletes RFC 2460.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

section.name: Example
section.t: Relays A and B are each configured to forward the namespace "live" to the other, and both use MAX_HOP_LIMIT 3. No publisher of "live" is connected. A subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE for ("live", "cam") to A without HOP_LIMIT.

figure.title: A two-relay cycle ending after three forwards
figure.artwork: Subscriber Relay A Relay B | | | |-- SUBSCRIBE -->| remaining = 3 | | |-- SUBSCRIBE ------>| remaining = 2 | | HOP_LIMIT = 2 | | |<-- SUBSCRIBE ------| | | HOP_LIMIT = 1 | | remaining = 1 < 3 (pending), so A forwards; it does not attach | |-- SUBSCRIBE ------>| remaining = 0 | | HOP_LIMIT = 0 | | |<- REQUEST_ERROR ---| HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED | |-- REQUEST_ERROR -->| (completes B's pending | | | request) | |<- REQUEST_ERROR ---| |<-REQUEST_ERROR-| | | HOP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED |

section.t: Without this extension, A and B forward the request to each other indefinitely, or, if they aggregate, wait on each other until a timeout.
